models.purpose: Express departing ball speed as a function of impact location, bat and ball properties, and swing state.

objectives: Predict outgoing ball speed for a specified collision state.
constraints: The impact point lies on the physical bat.
The brief-contact simplification sets I and L_imp approximately to zero in the main simulations.
The chosen restitution must remain physically admissible.

details: V_i, omega_i, v_i, impact location, and directions are supplied before contact.
Bat geometry bounds b and a short contact limits hand impulse.
The event is an impulse collision, not an equilibrium model.

parameter_estimation.method: Reference-bat measurements and literature values supply mass, inertia, speeds, and restitution; uncertainty is not propagated.

steps: Set geometry and pre-impact state.
Apply impulse and restitution equations.
Use the brief-contact approximation for the main case.
Evaluate v_f over impact locations and operating inputs.
algorithm.convergence_criteria: Not applicable to the closed-form solve; grid convergence for sweeps is not reported.

assumptions: Bat failure is excluded.
The bat is initially treated as rigid apart from restitution loss.
Hand linear and angular impulses are negligible during brief contact.
The main simulation uses a one-dimensional impact direction.

identifiability_feasibility.analysis: The closed system determines post-impact states when inputs are known, but restitution and human swing state are transferred from limited external evidence.

validation_refs: Pages 18-25 parameter sweeps and external comparisons.
Pages 40-42 revisit vibration through an effective restitution model.
models.computational_cost: Constant-time closed-form evaluation per collision state; sweep cost is linear in the number of grid points.
strengths: Uses physically interpretable impulse and restitution quantities.
Produces an explicit impact-location response suitable for optimization.
limitations: Free-body and rigid-response approximations are regime dependent.
No joint uncertainty or raw external validation data are supplied.
missing_details: Sign and angle conventions are not tested in executable unit cases.
Restitution calibration and measurement error are not reported.
Complete code for the fundamental model is absent.

models.purpose: Find the impact offset that maximizes BBS and distinguish it from a fixed center-of-percussion point.
models.summary: The BBS response is differentiated with respect to impact offset, yielding a quadratic stationarity condition and a selected positive physical root.

variables.definition: Distance from bat center of mass to the BBS-maximizing impact point.
Bat angular velocity before impact.
Incoming ball velocity under the paper sign convention.
Bat center-of-mass velocity before impact.
Mass of bat.
Mass of ball.
Bat inertia about its center of mass.

governing_equations.purpose: Stationarity condition obtained by differentiating BBS with respect to impact offset.
Selected physical root for the BBS-maximizing location.

equation_status.reason: The derivative condition and selected root are printed and visually checked.

objectives: Maximize v_f(b) over the physical bat impact interval.
constraints: b must lie between the handle-side and tip-side impact bounds.
The selected root must be real and consistent with the paper's velocity signs.
The stationary point must be compared with physical boundaries.

details: Pre-impact speeds and bat/ball properties are fixed for each optimization.
The finite bat length bounds b, although the paper does not formalize the feasible interval in the equation block.
Optimization is over an impulse response, not equilibrium.

parameter_estimation.method: Reference values and one-at-a-time ranges are taken from measurements or literature.

steps: Compute the quadratic roots.
Select the root consistent with the velocity signs.
Check it lies on the bat.
Evaluate BBS and compare with the tip across parameter sweeps.
algorithm.convergence_criteria: No iterative convergence; discretization density for validation plots is not reported.

assumptions: MU-A-2010-6749-001 remains valid.
BBS is the operational sweet-spot response.
Other performance dimensions do not enter the optimizer.

identifiability_feasibility.analysis: For known collision inputs the positive root is computable and can be checked against the physical interval; broader performance optimality is not demonstrated.

validation_refs: Pages 18-21 sweep pitch, translation, and rotation and compare the optimum with the bat tip.
models.computational_cost: Constant-time root evaluation per parameter state.
strengths: Defines the named feature through an explicit measurable optimum.
Shows directly why the optimum varies with operating conditions.
limitations: BBS alone does not represent comfort, control, injury, or fairness.
The paper does not provide a global certificate beyond the one-dimensional response.
missing_details: Explicit feasible bounds and endpoint comparison procedure.
Uncertainty interval for b.
A reproducible joint sensitivity analysis.

constraints: Material restitution coefficients remain within physical bounds.

parameter_estimation.method: Reference wood properties and standard material densities define the target and density ratio.

steps: Choose a candidate internal mass distribution.
Enforce total mass, first moment, and inertia constraints.

algorithm.convergence_criteria: No numerical design optimizer or manufacturability convergence rule is reported.

assumptions: Theoretical matching isolates material and trampoline effects.
The same outer shape and aggregate mechanics are feasible in aluminum.
Residual stiffness, damping, strength, grip, and manufacturing differences do not confound the comparison.

identifiability_feasibility.analysis: The constraints define infinitely many distributions; one special solution is shown, but nonnegativity, wall thickness, strength, and manufacturing feasibility are not fully demonstrated.

validation_refs: Pages 33-35 compare a theoretical matched design with external wood/metal batting data.
models.computational_cost: Constraint evaluation is linear in the representation size of m_z; no optimization cost is reported.
strengths: Uses a matched counterfactual to isolate the target material mechanism.
Makes mass, center, and inertia matching explicit rather than qualitative.
limitations: Infinite feasible distributions remain and engineering feasibility is not certified.
The external comparison cannot isolate all differences between real wood and metal bats.
missing_details: Nonnegative wall-thickness and strength constraints.
A solver for m_z and its convergence.
Prototype dimensions and test results.
Uncertainty in trampoline and controllability comparisons.
